### T0877

- **Topics:** the relational database management system (RDBMS) as a collection of tables with the ACID properties (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability; the theory is in U15.20) and the six techniques the primer lists to scale it: master-slave replication (the master serves reads and writes and replicates to slaves that serve reads, in a tree if needed; if the master fails the system runs read-only until a slave is promoted); master-master replication (both serve reads and writes and coordinate on writes; a load balancer or application logic decides where to write; loose consistency or higher write latency; conflict resolution) and the disadvantages of replication (possible data loss, replicas bogged down replaying writes, replication lag growing with more slaves, single-threaded replay, extra hardware); federation or functional partitioning (separate forums, users and products databases, less traffic and lag each, but joins across databases are harder and the application must know where to go); sharding (distribute data across databases so each holds a subset, such as users by last-name initial or by geography; less traffic, replication and index size and more cache hits; the disadvantages are application complexity, lopsided data from power users, rebalancing, hard joins; consistent hashing reduces the data moved); denormalization (redundant copies to avoid expensive joins, for example materialized views, since reads can outnumber writes 100:1 or 1000:1; the disadvantages are duplicated data and heavy-write cost); SQL tuning (benchmark with a load tool and profile with the slow query log; tighten the schema: CHAR for fixed length, TEXT for large text, INT up to 2^32, DECIMAL for currency, no large BLOBs, VARCHAR(255) and the 8-bit length, NOT NULL; use good indices (B-trees, extra space and slower writes, disabling indices during a bulk load); avoid expensive joins; partition tables; tune the query cache). NoSQL as key-value store (abstraction: hash table), document store (key-value store with documents as values, for example MongoDB, CouchDB and DynamoDB), wide column store (nested map of column families, row key and timestamp; Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra) and graph database (abstraction: graph); BASE (basically available, soft state, eventual consistency); SQL or NoSQL: the primer's reasons for SQL (structured data, strict schema, relational data, complex joins, transactions, clear patterns for scaling, established tools, fast index lookups) and for NoSQL (semi-structured data, dynamic or flexible schema, non-relational data, no complex joins, many TB or PB of data, data-intensive workload, very high IOPS throughput) and the sample data well-suited for NoSQL (clickstream and log ingest, leaderboard or scoring data, temporary data such as a shopping cart, hot tables, metadata and lookup tables).

### T0879

- **Topics:** why cache (shorter page loads, less load on servers and databases, absorbing uneven loads and spikes); where: client caching (the OS or browser), CDN caching, web server caching (reverse proxies and caches such as Varnish), database caching (default settings tuned to a generic load), application caching (in-memory key-value stores such as Memcached and Redis between the application and storage; Redis adds persistence and built-in data structures such as sorted sets and lists; avoid file-based caching because it hampers cloning and autoscaling); what: caching at the database query level (hash the query as the key; expiry is hard because one changed cell invalidates every cached query that might include it) and caching at the object level (assemble the data into a class instance, remove it when the underlying data changes, which also lets workers consume the latest cached object; suggested contents: user sessions, fully rendered web pages, activity streams, user graph data); when to update the cache: cache-aside (the application reads and writes storage and the cache stays passive: on a miss load from the database, add to the cache and return; lazy loading; each miss costs three trips and entries can go stale, limited by a TTL or write-through; a failed node is replaced by an empty one), write-through (the application writes to the cache as the main store and the cache writes synchronously to the data store; reads of just-written data are fast and data is not stale, but writes are slow and most written data might never be read), write-behind or write-back (add or update the cache and write to the store asynchronously; better write performance, risk of data loss if the cache fails first, more complex) and refresh-ahead (refresh recently accessed entries before they expire; lower latency if the access prediction is right, worse if it is wrong); the disadvantages of caches: keeping them consistent with the source of truth by cache invalidation, which is a hard problem, and changing the application.

### T0881

- **Topics:** asynchronism (expensive operations out of the request path, and work done in advance such as periodic aggregation): message queues (an application publishes a job and tells the user its status, a worker takes it, processes it and signals completion, while the client may show a small amount of optimistic work; Redis as a simple message broker whose messages can be lost, RabbitMQ with its AMQP protocol and self-managed nodes, Amazon SQS hosted but with higher latency and possible double delivery), task queues (receive tasks with data, run them and deliver results, with scheduling; Celery, mainly for Python), back pressure (a queue that outgrows memory means cache misses and disk reads, so limit the queue size and answer busy), and the disadvantage that cheap or real-time work is better synchronous. Communication: the hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) as a request and response protocol with a verb and a resource, and the verbs GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE with their idempotent, safe and cacheable columns; the transmission control protocol (TCP: connection-oriented, handshake, sequence numbers and checksums, retransmission, flow control, congestion control, many open connections costing memory, connection pooling; use it when all data must arrive intact); the user datagram protocol (UDP: connectionless datagrams that may arrive out of order or not at all, broadcast as with DHCP, no congestion control; use it for lowest latency, when late data is worse than lost data, or for your own error correction, as in VoIP, video chat, streaming and games); the remote procedure call (the call chain client program, client stub marshalling the procedure id and arguments, client and server communication modules, server stub unmarshalling and calling the server procedure, the reply in reverse; focused on exposing behaviours, tightly coupled, hard to debug and cache); representational state transfer (a client and server architecture on resources with stateless communication; four qualities: identify resources by a URI, change them through representations (verbs, headers and body), self-descriptive errors (status codes), and HATEOAS; focused on exposing data, usual for public APIs; its disadvantages: awkward when resources are not a simple hierarchy, few verbs, several round trips for nested data, payload bloat as fields grow); the table comparing RPC and REST calls (signup, resign, read a person, read a person's items, add an item, update an item, delete an item); security basics: encrypt in transit and at rest, sanitize all user inputs to prevent XSS and SQL injection, use parameterized queries, apply the principle of least privilege (the depth is in U5.18, U6.7 and U7.7).

### T0884

- **Topics:** the Primer's system design interview questions with solutions (Pastebin.com or Bit.ly, the Twitter timeline and search or Facebook feed and search, a web crawler, Mint.com, the data structures for a social network, a key-value store for a search engine, Amazon's sales ranking by category, scaling to millions of users on AWS), each worked in the same four steps: Step 1 outline use cases and constraints (use cases, out of scope, constraints and assumptions, state assumptions, calculate usage), Step 2 create a high level design, Step 3 design core components (one use case at a time), Step 4 scale the design, and then additional talking points (SQL scaling patterns, NoSQL, caching, asynchronism and microservices, communications, security, latency numbers). Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly): use cases: the user enters a block of text and gets a randomly generated link (with an optional expiration), the user enters a paste's url and views the contents, the service tracks analytics of pages (monthly visit statistics), the service deletes expired pastes, high availability; out of scope: accounts, email verification, editing, visibility, custom shortlinks; assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, following a short link should be fast, pastes are text only, analytics need not be realtime, 10 million users, 10 million paste writes and 100 million reads a month (10:1); usage: about 1.27 KB per paste (1 KB content, a 7-byte shortlink, a 4-byte expiration length, a 5-byte created-at, a 255-byte path), 12.7 GB a month, about 450 GB and 360 million shortlinks in 3 years, 4 writes and 40 reads per second. Core: a relational database as a large hash table from the url to a path on a file server, or an object store such as S3 or a NoSQL document or key-value store; the web server as a reverse proxy to a Write API and a Read API; the `pastes` table keyed on `shortlink`; the url from the MD5 hash of the user's IP address plus a timestamp, Base62-encoded (digits and letters, unlike Base64's `+` and `/`) and cut to the first 7 characters; a public REST API and RPC inside; analytics by MapReduce over the web server logs, and expiry by scanning for pastes older than the current timestamp; scaling: an analytics database (a data warehouse such as Redshift or BigQuery), an object store, a memory cache for the 40 reads a second, SQL write master-slave and the other SQL scaling patterns. Design the Twitter timeline and search (or Facebook feed and search): use cases: a user posts a tweet, views the home timeline (people followed), views the user timeline, searches keywords, with notifications and fan-out in scope; assumptions: 100 million active users, 500 million tweets a day (15 billion a month) with an average fan-out of 10 (5 billion deliveries a day), 250 billion reads and 10 billion searches a month, reads far outnumber writes; usage: about 10 KB per tweet (8-byte id, 32-byte user id, 140 bytes of text, about 10 KB of media), 150 TB a month and 5.4 PB in 3 years, 100 thousand reads, 6,000 tweets, 60 thousand fan-out deliveries and 4,000 searches a second. Core: the Write API stores the tweet in the user timeline (SQL) and calls the Fan Out Service, which asks the User Graph Service for followers (kept in the memory cache), pushes the tweet into each follower's home timeline in a Memory Cache (a Redis list of tweet id, user id and metadata, 17 bytes per entry), indexes it in the Search Index Service, stores media in the Object Store and sends push notifications through the Notification Service; the Read API asks the Timeline Service for the cached ids (O(1)) and does multiget calls to the Tweet Info and User Info Services (O(n)); search tokenises the query and asks a Search Cluster such as Lucene; scaling: the fan-out service is the bottleneck for users with millions of followers (so skip fan-out for them and merge their tweets in at read time), keep only a few hundred tweets per cached timeline and only active users' timelines (rebuild from SQL if inactive for 30 days), keep a month of tweets, keep the search index in memory, and add SQL scaling patterns.

### T0886

- **Topics:** Design a web crawler: use cases (the service crawls a list of urls, a user inputs a search term and sees pages with titles and snippets), assumptions (anonymous users, no infinite loop on a cyclic graph, 1 billion links to crawl and refreshed about weekly so 4 billion crawled a month, 500 KB per page, 100 billion searches a month, and no existing system such as Solr or Nutch), usage (2 PB a month, 72 PB in 3 years, 1,600 writes and 40,000 searches a second); core: ranked `links_to_crawl` (Redis sorted sets) and `crawled_links` with page signatures in a NoSQL store, a Crawler Service loop taking the top ranked link, classes PagesDataStore, Page and Crawler; handling duplicates (sort and unique for small lists, MapReduce keeping entries with frequency 1 for a billion links, and a content signature compared with the Jaccard index or cosine similarity); determining when to update the crawl results (a timestamp and a default one-week refresh, mean time between page changes, robots.txt); the search path (Query API, Reverse Index Service, Document Service); scaling (cache popular queries, shard and federate the index and document stores, the crawler's own DNS cache, connection pooling). Design Mint.com: use cases (the user connects to a financial account, the service extracts transactions from the account, the service recommends a budget, then the user accesses summaries and transactions), assumptions (10 million users with 10 budget categories each, 50,000 sellers, 30 million financial accounts, 5 billion transactions and 500 million reads a month, write-heavy 10:1, daily refresh for users active in the last 30 days), usage (about 50 bytes per transaction, 250 GB a month, 9 TB in 3 years, 2,000 writes and 200 reads a second); core: an Accounts API writing the `accounts` table, extraction through a queue (SQS or RabbitMQ) with a Transaction Extraction Service that stores raw logs in the object store, categorises through the Category Service (a seller-to-category dictionary, 50,000 sellers at under 255 bytes each, about 12 MB, with a heap of the top manual override per seller), and updates the `transactions` and `monthly_spending` tables; the Budget Service with a generic template by income tier (housing 40%, food 20%, gas 10%, shopping 20%) so only overrides are stored, aggregation in SQL or by MapReduce on the raw files; scaling (memory cache for sessions, aggregates and recent transactions, an analytics database such as Redshift or BigQuery, a month of transactions in the database and the rest in the object store). Design the data structures for a social network: use cases (a user searches for someone and sees the shortest path to the searched person), assumptions (graph data does not fit one machine, unweighted edges, 100 million users, 50 friends each so 5 billion friend relationships, 1 billion searches a month so 400 a second, no graph database or GraphQL), core: breadth-first search, with users sharded across Person Servers behind a Lookup Service and a User Graph Service running the search (classes Person, PersonServer, LookupService); further optimisations (cache complete or partial BFS traversals, batch offline into NoSQL, batch friend lookups on the same Person Server and shard by location, run two BFS searches from source and destination and merge, start from high-degree people, set a limit on time or hops before asking the user, or use a graph database such as Neo4j if allowed). Design a key-value store for a search engine: use case (a request that hits the cache), assumptions (popular queries nearly always cached, limited memory, millions of queries, 10 million users, 10 billion queries a month), usage (270 bytes per entry: 50-byte query, 20-byte title, 200-byte snippet; 2.7 TB a month if all unique; 4,000 requests a second); core: a memory cache with LRU expiry from a doubly linked list plus a hash table (classes Node, LinkedList, Cache), updated by TTL (cache-aside); scaling by expanding the memory cache to many machines in three ways (each machine its own cache, each with a copy, or the cache sharded by hashing the query). Design Amazon's sales ranking by category: use cases (the service calculates the past week's most popular products by category, a user views them), assumptions (10 million products, 1,000 categories, 1 billion transactions and 100 billion reads a month, 100:1, results updated hourly, items in several categories but never changing category), usage (about 40 bytes per transaction, 40 GB a month, 1.44 TB in 3 years, 400 writes and 40,000 reads a second), core: sales logs in the object store, a multi-step MapReduce (step 1 transform to `(category, product_id), sum(quantity)`, step 2 a distributed sort) writing a `sales_rank` table, read through the cache. Each of the five follows the template of U16.14: Outline use cases and constraints (use cases, out of scope, constraints and assumptions, state assumptions), Create a high level design, Design core components, Scale the design, and Additional talking points (SQL scaling patterns, NoSQL, caching, asynchronism, communications, security); the key-value cache design adds a Cache implementation section (the linked list, hash table and TTL update above).

### T0889

- **Topics:** Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS: use case: a user makes a read or write request; assumptions (relational data needed, 10 million users, 1 billion writes and 100 billion reads a month, 100:1, 1 KB per write), usage (1 TB a month, 36 TB in 3 years, 400 writes and 40,000 reads a second); Goals for 1-2 users: a single box, vertical scaling, and monitoring (CPU, memory, I/O, network; CloudWatch, top, Nagios, statsd, Graphite); start with a single box (web server and a MySQL database on one EC2 instance; vertical scaling gets expensive and has no redundancy); start with SQL, consider NoSQL; assign a public static IP (an elastic IP helps fail-over, since you point the domain at a new address); use a DNS (Route 53); secure the web server (open ports 80, 443 and 22 only from whitelisted IPs, no outbound connections). Scale the design in stages: Users+: assumptions (the single box is loaded, benchmarks and profiling point at MySQL), store static content separately in an object store (S3) and move the MySQL database to a separate box (RDS), secure the system (encrypt in transit and at rest, a virtual private cloud with a public subnet for the web server and a private one for the rest); Users++: horizontal scaling behind a load balancer (ELB or HAProxy, SSL terminated there), several web servers across availability zones, master-slave MySQL fail-over, separate web servers from application servers (a reverse proxy; read and write APIs), a CDN (CloudFront); Users+++ (read-heavy 100:1): a memory cache (Elasticache) for hot MySQL content and session data (so the web servers are stateless), add MySQL read replicas with a load balancer in front, and more servers; Users++++: add autoscaling (an autoscaling group per server type across zones, min and max sizes, triggers from CloudWatch on time of day, CPU load, latency, network traffic or a custom metric; the disadvantages are complexity and lag) and automate DevOps (Chef, Puppet, Ansible), with monitoring at host, aggregate, log, external-site, notification and error-reporting levels; Users+++++: keep iterating on benchmarks, a data warehouse (Redshift) for older data, and SQL scaling patterns and NoSQL. Additional system design interview questions, as the Primer lists them with reading: a file sync service like Dropbox, a search engine like Google, a scalable web crawler like Google, Google docs, a key-value store like Redis, a cache system like Memcached, a recommendation system like Amazon's, a tinyurl system like Bitly, a chat app like WhatsApp, a picture sharing system like Instagram, the Facebook news feed, the Facebook timeline, the Facebook chat function, a graph search function like Facebook's, a content delivery network like CloudFlare, a trending topic system like Twitter's, a random ID generation system, returning the top k requests during a time interval, a system that serves data from multiple data centers, an online multiplayer card game, a garbage collection system, an API rate limiter, and a stock exchange (like NASDAQ or Binance). Real-world architectures, by type: data processing (MapReduce, Spark, Storm), data store (Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, Spanner, Memcached, Redis), file system (the Google File System, HDFS) and miscellaneous (Chubby, Dapper, Kafka, ZooKeeper); company architectures (Amazon, Cinchcast, DataSift, Dropbox, ESPN, Google, Instagram, Justin.tv, Facebook, Flickr, Mailbox, Netflix, Pinterest, Playfish, PlentyOfFish, Salesforce, Stack Overflow, TripAdvisor, Tumblr, Twitter, Uber, WhatsApp, YouTube); and the company engineering blogs the Primer lists (for the companies you will meet). Under development in the source: distributed computing with MapReduce, consistent hashing and scatter gather. The AWS design uses the same template, so its sections read: Outline use cases and constraints, Use cases, Constraints and assumptions, Calculate usage, Create a high level design, Design core components, Additional talking points; the lists of real-world architectures also carry a misc group (the miscellaneous systems above).

### T0890

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Beyer et al., *Site Reliability Engineering*; Dean and Barroso 2013, "The tail at scale", recalled, not checked]* the company architectures and the engineering blogs are reading lists that were not opened or summarised for this curriculum; use them as sources for the design review, citing the page you used. ### T0891

- **Topics:** Introduction to Computing (the introductory course's Week 1): what a computer is (a machine that executes a stored program of instructions over data held in memory), the von Neumann organisation (processor, memory, input and output, with program and data in one memory), the layers from transistors and gates through the instruction set to the operating system and programs, and why everything is reduced to binary. Evolution of Computer Systems (the organisation course's Week 1): from mechanical calculators and the stored-program idea through vacuum tubes, transistors and integrated circuits to microprocessors and multicore chips; Moore's law as an observation about transistor counts and the end of Dennard scaling as the reason clock rates stopped rising and cores multiplied (history recalled, not checked). Number Systems (Week 2): binary representations and positional number systems in base 2, 8, 10 and 16, conversion between bases by repeated division and by grouping bits; unsigned integers and their range; signed representations: sign-magnitude, 1's complement (one's complement, with its two zeros) and 2's complement (two's complement); negation, sign extension, addition and subtraction of signed numbers and the overflow rule; bit-level operations (AND, OR, XOR, shifts, masks). Boolean algebra and gate-level logic: the axioms, De Morgan's laws, truth tables, sum-of-products and product-of-sums forms, Karnaugh-map minimisation, NAND and NOR as universal gates. Combinational building blocks: decoder, encoder, multiplexer, comparator, half and full adder, ripple-carry adder, a small ALU. Sequential logic: SR and D latches, edge-triggered D flip-flops, registers and counters, finite-state machines in Moore and Mealy form. Clocked timing: clock-to-Q delay, setup and hold times, the critical path and the maximum clock frequency, clock skew.

- **Build:** a gate-level simulator in Python (gates, then adders, a multiplexer, a 4-function ALU, D flip-flops and a register file) checked against Python integers on every input for small widths; a base converter and a signed-representation explorer; an exhaustive overflow-rule check at 6 bits; a sequence-detector state machine in Moore and Mealy form with a timing calculator for the critical path; the recomputation script `verify/v_b1.py` [check]. Real lab on the Mac: `uname -m` (expect `arm64`), then overflow and 2's complement experiments in C compiled with `clang` (unsigned wrap-around is defined, signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C, so the lab uses `-fwrapv` or the checked built-ins and says why), compared with the Python ALU (command names recalled, not checked; verify them first). [local]

### T0893

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Harris and Harris, Digital Design and Computer Architecture, ARM edition; Mano, Digital Design; recalled, not checked]* Karnaugh maps, state minimisation and the timing conditions are added because the source weeks give only titles; builds on U5.2 (arithmetic mod 2^n is the ring Z_n) and U2.11 (GF(2) and XOR). Outline map (the introductory course's outline, which says it will start out with a discussion on binary representations and a discussion on number systems, then move on to discuss assembly languages and computer arithmetic, and once we are done with the fundamentals look at the design of a simple processor, pipelining and memory): binary representations and number systems (1's complement and 2's complement) are taught here; assembly languages in U14.2; computer arithmetic in U14.4; the design of a simple processor in U14.5; concepts of pipelining in U14.6; the design of a modern memory system in U14.9 to U14.11.

### T0894

- **Topics:** Basic Computer Organization (the multicore course's Week 1): Review of Basic Computer Organization, Basic operational concepts (fetch, decode, execute, the program counter, the instruction and memory address registers), the fundamental of program execution (the instruction cycle and how a high-level statement becomes a sequence of instructions), memory and I/O addressing (byte addressing, alignment, little- and big-endian order; memory-mapped versus isolated I/O). Instruction Set Architecture (the organisation course's Week 2, and MCA Week 1): the instruction set as the contract between hardware and software; operand storage classes (stack, accumulator, register-memory, load-store); addressing modes (immediate, register, register indirect, base plus displacement, indexed, PC-relative, auto-increment as pre- and post-index); the instruction set itself (data transfer, arithmetic and logic, control flow, system); instruction encoding and formats (fixed versus variable length, field layout, expanding opcodes, immediates and their sign extension); CISC vs RISC ISA (the RISC principles: load-store, fixed-length encoding, many registers, simple addressing; the CISC trade-off of code density against decode complexity; modern x86 decoding into micro-operations, recalled, not checked). Assembly Language I and II (the introductory course's Weeks 4 and 5): registers and the zero register, arithmetic, logic and shift instructions, loads and stores, compare and conditional branches, loops and if-then-else, arrays and pointers, functions and procedure calls (branch-and-link, the return address, the stack and stack frames, caller- and callee-saved registers, the calling convention), recursion. Review of Traditional Computer Architecture (the GPU course's Week 1): the Basic five stage RISC Pipeline, Cache Memory, the Register File, and SIMD instructions, reviewed here from the instruction-set side and treated in depth in U14.6, U14.9 and U14.8. The teaching ISA: a small A64 (AArch64) subset of about 30 instructions (MOV, ADD, SUB, AND, ORR, EOR, LSL, LSR, MUL, SDIV, CMP, LDR, STR, LDP, STP, B, B.cond, CBZ, CBNZ, BL, RET, NOP), chosen because the learner's Mac runs it natively and it is a load-store RISC like the MIPS and RISC-V forms used by the sources.

### T0895

- **Crosswalk (A64 ↔ MIPS-like ↔ RISC-V-like; recalled, not checked, and the encodings below are recomputed by script):**

| Concept | A64 | MIPS-like | RISC-V-like |
|---|---|---|---|
| General registers | X0–X30 (64-bit), W0–W30 (low 32 bits); encoding 31 is XZR or SP by context | $0–$31, $zero hard-wired | x0–x31, x0 hard-wired zero |
| Register add | `ADD X0, X1, X2` = 0x8B020020 | `add $t0, $s1, $s2` = 0x02324020 | `add x10, x1, x2` = 0x00208533 |
| Immediate add | `ADD X0, X1, #imm12` (optionally shifted by 12) | `addi $t0, $s1, imm16` | `addi x10, x1, imm12` |
| Load and store | `LDR X0, [X1, #8]`; pre-index `[X1, #8]!`; post-index `[X1], #8`; pairs `LDP`/`STP` | `lw $t0, 8($s1)` | `ld x10, 8(x1)` |
| Compare and branch | `CMP X1, X2` sets NZCV, then `B.LT label` (19-bit word offset, ±1 MiB) | `slt` then `bne`/`beq` (16-bit word offset, ±128 KiB), with a delay slot | `blt x1, x2, label` (no flags) |
| Branch on zero | `CBZ X0, label` / `CBNZ` | `beq $t0, $zero, label` | `beqz x10, label` |
| Call and return | `BL f` puts the return address in X30; `RET` | `jal f` ($ra); `jr $ra` | `jal ra, f`; `ret` |
| Unconditional branch | `B label` (26-bit word offset, ±128 MiB) | `j target` (26-bit pseudo-direct) | `jal x0, label` |

### T0896

- **Results:** The four classes of operand storage and the RISC argument from instruction frequencies [S, from the measured dominance of simple instructions]; a branch field of k bits holding a signed word offset reaches ±2^{k−1}·4 bytes, so A64 `B` reaches ±128 MiB, `B.cond` and `CBZ` reach ±1 MiB with largest forward offset 1 048 572 bytes, and a MIPS `beq` reaches ±128 KiB [D]; the encodings in the crosswalk follow from the field layouts (MIPS R-type opcode 0, rs 17, rt 18, rd 8, funct 0x20 gives 0x02324020) [check]; an expanding opcode trades the number of operand fields against opcode space: in a 16-bit instruction of four 4-bit fields, using 15 primary opcode patterns for three-address instructions leaves one escape pattern for 16 two-address ones [D]; little-endian and big-endian orders agree on single bytes and differ by byte reversal on words [Def]; the procedure-call stack discipline (push the frame on entry, pop on exit) makes recursion work because each activation has its own frame [S]; memory-mapped I/O needs no extra instructions but uses address space, isolated I/O needs IN and OUT instructions [Def].

### T0898

- **Topics:** Performance Evaluation Methods (the multicore course's Week 2): response time and throughput, the iron law of processor performance, clock rate, instruction count and cycles per instruction (CPI), CPI of an instruction mix, MIPS and MFLOPS and why they mislead, benchmarks (synthetic, kernels, suites such as SPEC, recalled, not checked), summarising results by arithmetic, harmonic and geometric means, measurement method (repeat and take the minimum, warm-up, variance). Quantitative Principles of Computer Design (the organisation course's Week 3): make the common case fast; Amdahl's law applied to an enhancement of one part of the machine (speed-up is derived in U11.1 and only applied here); the principle of locality; take advantage of parallelism; trends in technology, power and cost (die cost and yield, recalled formula); dependability (MTTF, MTTR, availability).

### T0899

- **Results:** The iron law: time = instruction count × CPI × clock period [D]; CPI of a mix is Σ f_i·CPI_i, so the mix 45% ALU at 1, 25% loads at 4, 10% stores at 3 and 20% branches at 2 gives CPI 2.15 and 1488 MIPS at 3.2 GHz [D, check]; MIPS ranks machines wrongly when instruction counts differ [S, by a counterexample]; for equal work, the right mean of rates is the harmonic mean (1000 and 250 MIPS on equal work give 400, the total work over the total time) and the right mean of times is the arithmetic mean [P]; AM ≥ GM ≥ HM [P]; the geometric mean of normalised ratios is independent of the reference machine, since GM(a_i/r_i)/GM(b_i/r_i) = GM(a_i/b_i) [P]; Amdahl's law (proved in U11.1) applied: enhancing 40% of the time by a factor 10 gives 1.5625 overall [check]; availability = MTTF/(MTTF + MTTR) [Def]; dies per wafer ≈ π(d/2)²/A − πd/√(2A), giving about 416.8 for a 30 cm wafer and 1.5 cm² dies [check, formula recalled, not checked against a source].

### T0902

- **Topics:** Algorithms for Binary Addition (the introductory course's Week 6): ripple-carry, carry-select and carry-save addition; carry lookahead with generate g_i = a_i·b_i and propagate p_i = a_i ⊕ b_i; parallel prefix adders (Kogge–Stone, Brent–Kung) as the associative operator (g, p)∘(g′, p′) = (g + p·g′, p·p′); subtraction through 2's complement. Algorithms for Multiplication and Division (Week 7): shift-and-add multiplication, Booth's algorithm (radix-2 and radix-4 recoding), array multipliers, Wallace and Dadda tree reduction with 3:2 counters; restoring and non-restoring division, SRT division (stated). Floating Point Numbers (Week 3): scientific notation in base 2; the IEEE 754 formats (binary32, binary64) with sign, biased exponent and fraction; normal and subnormal (denormal) numbers, zeros, infinities and NaNs; rounding modes (round to nearest even, toward zero, toward ±∞) with guard, round and sticky bits; floating-point addition (align, add, normalise, round) and multiplication; the loss of associativity and catastrophic cancellation. Design of Arithmetic Unit (the organisation course's Weeks 7 and 8, contd.): the integer ALU with fast adders, the multiplier and divider units, the floating-point unit and how they are pipelined.

### T0904

- **Topics:** Processor Design (the introductory course's Week 8): the datapath elements (program counter, instruction memory, register file with two read ports and one write port, sign extender, ALU, data memory, multiplexers), building a single-cycle datapath for the A64 subset (R-type, load, store, branch and branch-and-link), the main control and the ALU control, control-signal tables, the critical path of the single-cycle design; the multi-cycle datapath with instruction register and intermediate registers, its finite-state control, CPI of the multi-cycle design. Control Unit Design (the organisation course's Week 4): hardwired control from a state machine; microprogrammed control with a control store, microinstruction formats (horizontal and vertical), sequencing (next-address field, dispatch tables, a microprogram counter); comparison of hardwired versus microprogrammed control in speed, flexibility and design effort; exceptions and interrupts in the control unit (the exception program counter, the cause register).

### T0905

- **Topics:** Instruction Pipeline Principles (the multicore course's Week 2): Introduction to RISC Instruction Pipeline (the classic five stages IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB with pipeline registers between them), Instruction Pipeline and Performance (throughput versus latency, the ideal speed-up, pipeline register overhead and unbalanced stages), Pipeline Hazards and Analysis (structural, data and control hazards; RAW, WAR and WAW dependences and which of them can cause hazards in an in-order pipeline). Pipelining I and II (the introductory course's Weeks 9 and 10) and Instruction Set Pipelining (the organisation course's Week 11, titled "Instruction Set Pipelining" in the source; the standard name is instruction pipelining): the pipelined datapath and its control, forwarding (bypassing) paths and the forwarding unit, the hazard-detection unit and the load-use stall, interlocks versus compiler-scheduled delay slots, branch resolution in ID with a flush, precise exceptions in a pipeline. In-order pipelines overview (the advanced course's Week 1): deeper and wider in-order pipelines, the cost of deep pipelines, the optimal pipeline depth. Pipeline Hazards and Branch Prediction Techniques (MCA Week 3): Pipeline Hazards Management Techniques (stalling, forwarding, scheduling, predict-not-taken, delayed branches), Branch Prediction (static prediction, backward-taken forward-not-taken, one-bit and two-bit saturating counters, the branch target buffer and return address stack), MIPS Pipeline for Multi-Cycle Operations (floating-point units of different latencies, the structural hazard on the write port, WAW hazards and out-of-order completion, and the resulting precise-exception problem). Branch prediction (the advanced course's Week 2) and Advanced branch prediction techniques (Week 3): correlating (two-level) predictors with global and local history, gshare, tournament predictors that choose between predictors, and the TAGE and perceptron predictors (stated; recalled, not checked).

### T0906

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Hennessy and Patterson, Appendix C and Chapter 3; Yeh and Patt (1991) on two-level prediction; McFarling (1993) on gshare and combining predictors; Seznec on TAGE; Jiménez and Lin (2001) on perceptron prediction; Hartstein and Puzak (2002) on optimal pipeline depth; recalled, not checked]* uses U2.1 (Markov chains) for the predictor model.

### T0907

- **Topics:** Pipeline Scheduling and Speculative execution (the multicore course's Week 4): Compiler Techniques to Explore Instruction Level Parallelism (basic-block scheduling, loop unrolling with register renaming by the compiler, software pipelining and modulo scheduling, trace and superblock scheduling, predication), Dynamic Scheduling with Tomasulo's Algorithm (reservation stations, the common data bus, tags and register renaming that remove WAR and WAW hazards; the scoreboard of the CDC 6600 as the earlier scheme), Speculative Execution (executing past unresolved branches, the reorder buffer, in-order commit, misprediction recovery and precise exceptions). Out-of-order pipelines (the advanced course's Week 2): the front end, rename, the issue queue, the physical register file versus ROB-based renaming, the load-store queue. Issue, select, and commit (Week 4): wake-up and select logic, issue-queue organisation, the commit stage, retirement width, recovery by walking the ROB or checkpoints of the rename table. Aggressive speculation (Week 5): memory dependence prediction (store sets), load speculation and replay, value prediction, and speculation's cost in wasted energy. Compiler techniques for enhancing ILP (Week 6): dependence analysis, loop unrolling, software pipelining with the minimum initiation interval, trace scheduling, VLIW and EPIC as the static alternative. The relation between dynamic hardware scheduling and static compiler scheduling, and the limits of ILP.

### T0908

- **Topics:** Superscalar Processors and GPU architectures (the multicore course's Week 5): Advanced Pipelining (multiple issue, static versus dynamic superscalar, VLIW), Superscalar Processors (fetch of several instructions per cycle, decode and rename of a group with intra-group dependence checks, wide issue, the cost of wide bypass networks and register-file ports), Multithreading and Hyperthreading (fine-grained, coarse-grained and simultaneous multithreading; hyperthreading as Intel's name for SMT; thread selection policies; the resources shared and replicated), and GPU Architectures (introduced here as the extreme of throughput-oriented multithreading and taught in U14.17). SIMD instructions (from the GPU course's Week 1 review of traditional computer architecture): packed data types and vector lanes, the Arm NEON (Advanced SIMD) 128-bit registers, vector length, strip mining, masked or tail handling, vector architectures with vector registers and chaining as the historical form, and the Register File as the shared resource of wide and multithreaded cores. Heterogeneous cores: performance and efficiency cores on Apple silicon (recalled, not checked).

### T0909

- **Topics:** Cache Memory Principles (the multicore course's Week 6): Introduction to Cache Memory (the principle of locality, temporal and spatial; the hierarchy of registers, caches, main memory and storage; hit, miss, hit time and miss penalty), Block Replacement Techniques and Write Strategy (random, FIFO, LRU and pseudo-LRU, Belady's optimal policy; write-through with write buffers versus write-back with dirty bits; write-allocate versus no-write-allocate), Design Concepts in Cache Memory (block placement by direct mapping, set associativity and full associativity; block identification by tag, index and offset; the valid bit; split versus unified caches; inclusion and exclusion between levels). Cache Memory Optimizations (Week 7): Design issues for improving memory access time, Basic and Advanced Optimization Techniques in Cache Memory: larger blocks, larger caches and higher associativity, multilevel caches, giving reads priority over writes, avoiding address translation during indexing; small and simple first-level caches, way prediction, pipelined and non-blocking caches (miss status holding registers), multibanked caches, critical word first and early restart, merging write buffers, compiler optimisations (loop interchange, blocking), hardware and software prefetching, victim caches (recalled list, not checked). Memory System Design (the organisation course's Week 5): memory chips and their organisation, building a larger memory from smaller chips by width and depth expansion with an address decoder, memory interleaving; Design of Cache Memory Systems (Week 6). Memory Systems: Caches (the introductory course's Week 11). Caches: Design, modeling, and optimizations (the advanced course's Week 7): analytic miss models, the 3C model (compulsory, capacity, conflict), reuse distance and stack algorithms. Memory Hierarchy: Cache and Virtual memory (the parallel architecture course's Week 3): the cache half here, the virtual-memory half in U14.10. The same replacement and write policies appear in software caches in U16.12.

### T0910

- **Results:** For a cache of size S, associativity A and line size B with a-bit addresses, offset = log₂ B, index = log₂(S/(A·B)), tag = a − index − offset: 32 KiB, 8-way, 64 B lines and 48-bit addresses give 36/6/6, and 128 KiB, 8-way, 128 B lines give 34/7/7 [D, check]; AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, and for two levels AMAT = t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_mem) with m₂ the local miss rate, so 1 + 0.05(10 + 0.2·100) = 2.5 cycles [D, check]; tag, valid and dirty storage for the first example is 38 bits per 512 data bits, 7.4% [check]; LRU is a stack algorithm: the contents of an LRU cache of capacity c are always a subset of those of capacity c + 1, so misses never increase with capacity [P, check]; FIFO is not a stack algorithm and shows Belady's anomaly (the trace 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 has 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4) [check]; Belady's MIN (evict the block used furthest in the future) is optimal [P, by an exchange argument] and never worse than LRU or FIFO [check]; the 3C classification: compulsory misses are first references, capacity misses are the further misses of a fully associative LRU cache of the same size, and conflict misses are the rest [Def, check on a direct-mapped example: 5, 0 and 3]; a 64K × 8 memory built from 16K × 4 chips needs 8 chips in four banks of two selected by a 2-to-4 decoder [D, check]; LRU hit ratio under a Zipf workload follows Che's approximation (the analytic models are owned by U3.11, which derives Che's approximation, and U10.6, which gives the Zipf harmonic-sum ratio), which this unit uses as an oracle: for N = 1000 objects, capacity 100 and exponent 0.8 the approximation and a simulation agree within 0.01 [check].

### T0913

- **Topics:** Virtual Memory (the introductory course's Week 12): the virtual address space and the physical address space, pages and page frames, the page table and page-table entries (valid, dirty, referenced, protection and execute-never bits), multi-level (hierarchical) page tables, inverted and hashed page tables, the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) and its organisation, TLB misses handled by a hardware page-table walker or by software, page faults and demand paging, replacement and the working set, protection between processes and between user and kernel, address-space identifiers so that a context switch need not flush the TLB, large pages (superpages) and TLB reach, and the interaction of the cache with translation (physically indexed physically tagged, virtually indexed physically tagged, aliasing and synonyms). Memory Hierarchy: Cache and Virtual memory (the parallel architecture course's Week 3): the virtual-memory half here, the cache half in U14.9; translation as one more level of the hierarchy whose "miss penalty" is a table walk or a disk access.

### T0914

- **Results:** A single-level table for a 48-bit virtual address with 8-byte entries costs 2³⁴ × 8 B = 128 GiB with 16 KiB pages and 512 GiB with 4 KiB pages, which is why tables are hierarchical [D, check]; with page size 2^g and 8-byte entries each level resolves g − 3 bits, so 4 KiB pages give 9 bits per level and four levels for 48 bits, and 16 KiB pages give 11 bits per level, three levels covering 47 bits (14 + 3 × 11) and a fourth two-entry level for 48 bits [D, check]; TLB reach = entries × page size, so 2048 entries reach 32 MiB with 16 KiB pages but only 8 MiB with 4 KiB pages [D, check]; a virtually indexed physically tagged cache avoids synonyms when cache size / associativity ≤ page size, so a 128 KiB 8-way L1 fits 16 KiB pages and a 32 KiB L1 with 4 KiB pages needs 8 ways [D, check]; with memory access 100 ns and fault service 8 ms, keeping the effective access time within 10% of a fault-free one needs a fault rate below 10/(8 × 10⁶ − 100) ≈ 1.25 × 10⁻⁶ [D, check]; the effective-access-time formula hit·t + (1 − hit)(t + k·t) is owned by U4.1, and this unit's MMU simulator reproduces it as an oracle (simulated and formula values within 2 ns at hit ratios 0.9 and 0.98) [check]; the nested-walk cost (n + 1)(m + 1) − 1, 24 references for four-level guest and host tables, is owned by U4.2 [D, check].

### T0916

- **Topics:** Primary Storage Systems (the multicore course's Week 9): Introduction to DRAM System (the one-transistor one-capacitor cell, destructive reads and sense amplifiers, refresh), DRAM organization (channels, ranks, chips, bank groups, banks, rows, columns; the row buffer as a cache of one row; the commands ACTIVATE, READ, WRITE, PRECHARGE and REFRESH; the timing parameters tCL, tRCD, tRP, tRAS, tRC, tFAW and tREFI; synchronous DRAM and double data rate), DRAM Controllers and Address Mapping (open-page and closed-page policies, request queues and schedulers such as FCFS and FR-FCFS, bank-level parallelism, mapping of physical address bits to channel, rank, bank, row and column, and interleaving to spread consecutive lines across banks). The advanced course's outline places this among the main memory technologies such as DDR-4, after cache design; this unit treats DDR4 as the worked standard and notes LPDDR (used in the unified memory of Apple-silicon systems) and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) as variants (recalled, not checked). Map of the advanced course's outline, which says the course will introduce students to advanced aspects of processor design, will specifically focus on out-of-order pipelines, GPUs, and compiler techniques for enhancing ILP, will subsequently move on to cache design and main memory technologies such as DDR-4, will devote a substantial portion of the course to the theory of on-chip networks and memory models, and will in its last part cover aspects of low-power design, hardware security, and reliability: processor design, out-of-order pipelines and compiler techniques for ILP are taught in U14.6 and U14.7; GPUs in U14.8 and U14.17; cache design in U14.9; main memory technologies here; the theory of on-chip networks in U14.16; memory models in U14.15; quality of service and emerging directions in U14.21; low-power design, hardware security and reliability in U14.22.

### T0918

- **Topics:** Input-Output System Design (the organisation course's Weeks 9 and 10, with "contd." for the second week): I/O devices and controllers, memory-mapped versus isolated (port-mapped) I/O, device registers (status, control, data), programmed I/O with polling, interrupt-driven I/O (interrupt request and acknowledge, vectored interrupts, priority and daisy chaining, nesting and masking, interrupt latency), direct memory access (the DMA controller, cycle stealing versus burst mode, descriptor rings and scatter-gather), buses (synchronous and asynchronous protocols, handshaking, bus width and clock, multiplexed address and data lines, split transactions), bus arbitration (centralised daisy chain, centralised parallel, distributed), the hierarchy of buses and point-to-point links (a processor-memory interconnect, PCI Express lanes, USB), storage interfaces (magnetic disk organisation into platters, tracks and sectors; seek, rotational latency and transfer time; flash solid-state drives and NVMe as a contrast), and I/O performance measures (throughput and response time).

### T0919

- **Topics:** Introduction to Parallel Architectures (the parallel architecture course's Week 1): why parallel computing has become a critical component, driven by application domains requiring large data processing as well as faster compute performance; the use of multi-core processors as well as tightly integrated clusters of PCs and workstations; Flynn's taxonomy (SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD); shared-memory multiprocessors (UMA and NUMA) and distributed-memory multicomputers; the convergence of traditionally disparate approaches of shared memory, message passing, and data driven computing onto the same platform, with dataflow as the data-driven model; communication architecture as the boundary between programming model and hardware. Parallel Programming models and Architectures (Week 2): the shared address space model (threads, loads and stores, locks and barriers), the message-passing model (send and receive, synchronous and asynchronous), the data-parallel model (SIMD and SPMD), the steps of creating a parallel program (decomposition, assignment, orchestration, mapping), communication-to-computation ratio and load balance. Parallel Processing Architectures (the organisation course's Week 12): pipelined, vector and array processors, multiprocessors and multicomputers, and performance measures for parallel systems. Map of the parallel architecture course's outline: the parallel applications communicate with each other using shared data, so it is important to correctly manage the shared data within the memory hierarchy to avoid inconsistency; we need to understand the mechanisms used for data access, communication and coordination of work and its correct implementation, and the in-depth shared memory management for parallel architectures, are in U14.14 (coherence) and U14.15 (consistency and synchronisation); the interconnection topologies and routing methods which are important for connection and communication of the multiple cores executing the parallel applications are in U14.16; the overview of various parallel architectures and on-going research directions is here and in U14.21. Map of the multicore course's outline: mobile gadgets and applications, crucial to maintaining comfort in modern living, and the apps supported by portable electronic devices with powerful microprocessors, and the era of multi-core systems where even the simplest of handheld devices like a smart phone houses many processors in a single chip motivate this unit, as do core counts ever increasing from 8 to 10 in smart phones to over 100s in super computers; the world of multi-core computer architectures with on-chip storage systems and inter-core communication framework, given equal attention as that of processors with the unprecedented growth of data science, run through D14; the fundamentals of basic computer organization are in U14.1 to U14.5; multicore processors in U14.8 and U14.14; GPUs in U14.17; advanced cache memory optimizations in U14.9; DRAM systems in U14.11; on chip interconnects in U14.16; domain specific accelerators in U14.20; current research standings and on-going research directions in U14.21.

### T0920

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Culler, Singh and Gupta, Parallel Computer Architecture: A Hardware/Software Approach; Flynn (1972); Karp and Flatt (1990); Brent (1974); Blumofe and Leiserson on work stealing; recalled, not checked]* links to U9.9 (distributed shared memory in software) and U11.1 (scaling laws).

### T0921

- **Topics:** Cache Coherence Protocols (the multicore course's Week 8): Cache coherence and memory consistency (the coherence problem as two caches holding different values for one location; coherence as the single-writer multiple-reader invariant plus the data-value invariant, against consistency as the ordering of accesses to different locations, treated in U14.15), Snoop Based and Directory Based Cache coherence Protocols. Coherence Protocols (the advanced course's Week 10). Overview of Cache coherence, Coherence Protocols- Snooping, Directory based protocols, VI protocol (the parallel architecture course's Week 4): the two-state valid–invalid protocol for write-through caches. MSI, MESI, Dragon protocol and Correctness of coherence protocols- Types of cache misses, update vs invalidate protocol (Week 5): the three-state MSI protocol with bus read, bus read-exclusive and upgrade transactions; MESI with the exclusive-clean state; the Dragon update protocol with states exclusive-clean, shared-clean, shared-modified and modified; the four Cs (compulsory, capacity, conflict and coherence misses, with coherence misses split into true sharing and false sharing); invalidate versus update. Snoop based muliprocessor design (source spelling, Weeks 6 and 7), Single and multi-level cache with atomic bus: race conditions, transient states, the snoop tag and the dual-tagged cache, inclusion between levels; Single and multi-level cache with split transaction bus: a request table, outstanding transactions, ordering and flow control on the bus. Scalable shared memory systems: Directory coherence protocols- Memory based, cache based, correctness (Week 8): full bit-vector and limited-pointer directories at the home node, cache-based (distributed linked-list) directories, three-hop and four-hop transactions, reply forwarding, serialisation at the home and avoidance of deadlock and livelock. Case study: Origin- Architecture, protocol, correctness; Sequent NUMA Q- Architecture, protocol, correctness (Week 9): the SGI Origin 2000 memory-based directory with hubs and reply forwarding, and the Sequent NUMA-Q cache-based directory built on the Scalable Coherent Interface (SCI) doubly linked sharing lists (recalled, not checked).

### T0922

- **Results:** An exhaustive model checker over abstract states with an atomic bus finds 6 reachable global states for MSI with two caches and 11 with three, and 8 and 14 for MESI, and confirms the single-writer multiple-reader invariant in all of them, while a deliberately broken protocol whose writes do not invalidate is caught [check]; reading and then writing private data costs two bus transactions under MSI (bus read, then upgrade) and one under MESI, whose exclusive-to-modified transition is silent [D, check]; a full bit-vector directory with two state bits per 64-byte block costs (P + 2)/512 of memory, 12.9% at 64 cores and 50.4% at 256, while four 8-bit pointers at 256 cores cost 6.6% [D, check]; when a producer writes a line k times before one consumer reads it, invalidation costs two transactions and update costs k, so update wins only for k < 2 (fine-grained producer–consumer sharing) [D, check]; with a 100-cycle memory, a split-transaction bus that frees the bus between request (1 cycle) and response (4 cycles) carries 21 times the transactions of an atomic bus that holds it throughout [D, check]; under MSI two cores that alternately write different words of one line suffer one coherence miss per write (1000 for 1000 writes), and padding the words onto different lines leaves two compulsory misses [check]; directory correctness needs serialisation of requests per line at the home node and a protocol whose message classes travel on separate virtual networks so that requests cannot block replies [D].

### T0924

### T0925

- **Topics:** Theory of memory models (the advanced course's Week 9): a memory model as the set of values a load may return; program order, the global memory order and the "reads from" relation; sequential consistency as some total order consistent with every program order; total store order (TSO, the x86 model) with store buffers and forwarding; relaxed models (release consistency, the ARM and RISC-V weak models) that let independent accesses be reordered unless ordered by fences, acquire and release, or dependencies; litmus tests (store buffering SB, message passing MP, load buffering LB, independent reads of independent writes IRIW) and axiomatic versus operational definitions. Memory consistency models- Sequential, Relaxed consistency models (the parallel architecture course's Week 10): Lamport's definition, the conditions program order and write atomicity, how write buffers, non-blocking caches and out-of-order execution break sequential consistency, and the processor-consistency, weak-ordering and release-consistency families. Synchronization- LL-SC, point to point, barrier synchronization (Week 11): atomic read-modify-write instructions (test-and-set, swap, fetch-and-add, compare-and-swap), load-linked and store-conditional, test-and-test-and-set, ticket and queue-based (MCS) locks, point-to-point synchronisation with flags, centralised sense-reversing, tree and dissemination barriers. Cache coherence and memory consistency (the multicore course's Week 8): the consistency half here, the coherence half in U14.14.

### T0926

- **Results:** A litmus-test enumerator finds that SB has three outcomes under sequential consistency, with r1 = r2 = 0 forbidden, while an operational TSO model with FIFO store buffers and forwarding allows r1 = r2 = 0 [check]; MP's outcome (flag seen, data stale) is forbidden under TSO and allowed under a relaxed model that may reorder accesses to different addresses, and a fence between the two accesses in each thread restores the sequentially consistent outcome sets of both tests [check]; two threads of m and n accesses have C(m + n, m) interleavings, 6 for SB and 20 for three accesses each [D, check]; a data-race-free program behaves sequentially consistently on any model that honours its synchronisation (the DRF-SC guarantee) [P, recalled]; LL/SC implements any read-modify-write and avoids the ABA problem of compare-and-swap because the store fails after any intervening write to the line [D]; a contended test-and-test-and-set lock costs O(P) bus transactions per release and about P(P + 1)/2 for P successive hand-offs (36 at P = 8), whereas a ticket lock needs one atomic operation per acquisition (its waiters still re-read the counter after each release) and an MCS lock causes O(1) traffic per hand-off because each waiter spins on its own flag [D, check]; a dissemination barrier needs ⌈log₂ P⌉ rounds, 6 at 64 and 7 at 100 threads [D, check]. Relation to distributed consistency: U14.15 owns hardware memory models and U9.16 owns distributed consistency (linearizability, CAP, quorums); sequential consistency is the hardware counterpart of Lamport's definition used in U9.16, TSO resembles a per-process ordered (FIFO) model, and fences play the role that synchronisation operations play in weak distributed models.

### T0927

- **Build:** a litmus enumerator for SC, TSO and a relaxed model that reproduces the allowed-outcome tables for SB, MP, LB and IRIW with and without fences [check]; LL/SC, ticket, MCS and barrier implementations on the emulator of U14.5 extended with a store buffer, and the DSim scheduler of U9.1 reused to explore thread interleavings. Real lab on the Mac: **litmus tests on real hardware**: store-buffering and message-passing tests in C with two threads over many iterations (millions), counting each outcome; observe the relaxed outcomes that a weakly ordered ARM core allows, then add `atomic_thread_fence` or acquire–release atomics and see them vanish; compare with your enumerator. ### T0928

- **Topics:** Tiled Chip Multi-Core Processors & Network-on-Chip (the multicore course's Week 10): Tiled Chip Multicore Processors (TCMP), Network on Chips (NoC), Routing Algorithms, NoC router – architecture (input buffers, virtual channels, route computation, virtual-channel allocation, switch allocation, the crossbar, and the pipeline of these stages with lookahead and speculation), Routing and flow control (store-and-forward, virtual cut-through and wormhole switching; credit-based and on–off back-pressure). Energy Efficient NoCs (Week 11): Introduction to deflection routing (hot-potato routing in which every arriving flit leaves on some port each cycle), Energy Efficient Buffer-less NoC Routers (removing input buffers to save area and power, at the cost of deflections at high load), Side-buffered Deflection Routers (a small side buffer that absorbs some deflected flits). On-chip networks (the advanced course's Week 8): topology metrics (degree, diameter, average hop count, bisection bandwidth), deadlock and livelock, the channel dependency graph, the turn model. Interconnects- Introduction, Topologies, routing, flow control (the parallel architecture course's Week 12): direct and indirect networks (ring, mesh, torus, hypercube, butterfly, fat tree), deterministic, oblivious and adaptive routing, and latency and throughput models.

### T0929

- **Topics:** GPU architectures - Streaming Multi Processors, Cache Hierarchy, The Graphics Pipeline (the GPU course's Week 2): the GPU as a throughput processor; the streaming multiprocessor (SM) with its warp schedulers, SIMD lanes (CUDA cores), special-function and load-store units, register file and shared memory; the generalisation of SIMD into single instruction multiple thread (SIMT) execution, in which a warp of 32 threads shares one instruction stream; the cache hierarchy (per-SM L1 and shared memory, a texture and a constant cache, a shared L2, and high-bandwidth DRAM); the graphics pipeline (vertex processing, primitive assembly, rasterisation, fragment processing, raster operations) and the move from fixed-function stages to unified programmable shaders. Warp Scheduling, Divergence (Week 5): warps as the unit of scheduling, latency hiding by switching among resident warps, schedulers such as loose round-robin and greedy-then-oldest, occupancy and the resources that limit it (threads, blocks, registers, shared memory), branch divergence within a warp, the active mask, the reconvergence stack and immediate post-dominator reconvergence. GPU Architectures (the multicore course's Week 5): the GPU half of that week, the superscalar and multithreading half in U14.8.

### T0930

- **Build:** a SIMT execution simulator with warps, an active mask, a reconvergence stack, a round-robin warp scheduler and a memory latency, which reports cycles and SIMD efficiency for branching kernels, and an occupancy calculator for stated resource limits [check]. Real lab: simulation first, then a vocabulary map from the CUDA terms to Apple's Metal terms (thread to thread, warp to SIMD-group, block to threadgroup, shared memory to threadgroup memory, `__syncthreads` to `threadgroup_barrier`; the Apple SIMD-group width is recalled as 32, recalled, not checked). Fallback logic: (1) check whether a GPU route is available (`torch.backends.mps.is_available()` for the Mac, or a Colab or Kaggle notebook on a personal account if you want a real warp-level divergence measurement); (2) if so, time a divergent and a warp-uniform kernel and record the numbers; (3) if not, run the same kernels on the SIMT simulator and say so. ### T0931

- **Topics:** Introduction to CUDA programming (the GPU course's Week 3): the host and the device, kernels and the `__global__` qualifier, launching a grid of blocks of threads, device memory allocation and copies, error checking, the built-in variables threadIdx, blockIdx, blockDim and gridDim. Multi-dimensional mapping of dataspace, Synchronization (Week 4): one-, two- and three-dimensional grids and blocks, mapping a thread to an element of a matrix or image, bounds checks for sizes that are not multiples of the block, grid-stride loops; `__syncthreads` within a block, why there is no barrier across blocks inside a kernel, atomic operations. Memory Access Coalescing (Week 6): how the loads of a warp are combined into 32-byte sectors and 128-byte lines, unit-stride versus strided and misaligned access, structure-of-arrays versus array-of-structures, shared-memory tiling and bank conflicts. Optimization examples : optimizing Reduction Kernels (Week 7): interleaved addressing with divergent branches, interleaved addressing with bank conflicts, sequential addressing, first add during load, unrolling the last warp, complete unrolling and multiple elements per thread (the classic sequence of seven versions, recalled, not checked). Optimization examples : Kernel Fusion, Thread and Block (Week 8): fusing element-wise kernels to remove intermediate global traffic, choosing block size and grid size, thread coarsening. Map of the GPU course's outline: the course covers basics of conventional CPU architectures (U14.5 to U14.9), their extensions for single instruction multiple data processing (SIMD) (U14.8) and finally the generalization of this concept in the form of single instruction multiple thread processing (SIMT) as is done in modern GPUs (U14.17); we cover GPU architecture basics in terms of functional units in U14.17 and then dive into the popular CUDA programming model commonly used for GPU programming here; in this context, architecture specific details like memory access coalescing, shared memory usage, GPU thread scheduling etc which primarily effect (source spelling) program performance are also covered in detail here and in U14.17; we next switch to a different SIMD programming language called OpenCL which can be used for programming both CPUs and GPUs in a generic manner in U14.19; the different architectureaware (source spelling) optimization techniques relevant to both CUDA and OpenCL run through U14.18 and U14.19; finally, where the outline says we provide the students with detail application development examples in two well-known GPU computing scenarios, those examples (efficient neural-network training and inference) are in U14.20.

### T0932

- **Topics:** OpenCL basics (the GPU course's Week 9): the platform model (a host and compute devices made of compute units made of processing elements), the execution model (an NDRange of work-items grouped into work-groups; get_global_id, get_local_id, get_group_id), the memory model (global, constant, local and private memory), contexts, command queues, buffers, programs compiled at run time from kernel source, kernel arguments and events; the correspondence with CUDA (work-item to thread, work-group to block, local memory to shared memory, NDRange to grid). OpenCL for Heterogeneous Computing (Week 10): one kernel source for CPUs and GPUs, device discovery and selection, in-order and out-of-order queues with event dependencies, overlapping transfer and computation, partitioning work between a CPU and a GPU, and the host-to-device copy cost of a discrete GPU, against shared (unified) memory on integrated GPUs.

### T0933

- **Topics:** Domain Specific Accelerators (the multicore course's Week 12; the quality-of-service and emerging-trends parts of that week are in U14.21): why specialisation pays when general-purpose scaling slows (energy per operation dominated by data movement), the roofline model and arithmetic intensity, systolic arrays (weight-, output- and input-stationary dataflows), tensor-processing units and tensor cores, on-chip buffers and reuse, near-memory processing. Application Design : Efficient Neural Network Training/Inferencing (the GPU course's Weeks 11 and 12, with "Contd.," for the second): counting MACs, parameters and activation memory of convolution and fully connected layers; mapping convolution to matrix multiplication (im2col); mixed-precision training with loss scaling; quantisation (scale and zero point, symmetric and asymmetric, per-tensor and per-channel), post-training quantisation and quantisation-aware training; pruning, sparsity and knowledge distillation; batching for throughput against latency; operator fusion; inference on integrated and mobile GPUs.

### T0934

- **Topics:** Quality of Service for TCMPs: QoS of NoC and Caches in TCMPs (the multicore course's Week 12; the domain-specific-accelerator part of that week is in U14.20): why a shared last-level cache and a shared on-chip network let one application slow another, and how to measure it (slowdown against running alone, weighted speed-up, harmonic speed-up, maximum-to-minimum slowdown as unfairness); cache way-partitioning, utility-based partitioning driven by per-application miss curves, and the greedy marginal-utility allocator; page colouring as a software partition of sets; NoC arbitration for QoS: round-robin, weighted round-robin, age-based and priority arbitration, virtual-channel reservation, and frame-based schemes that give each source a bandwidth share per frame; the relation to network QoS, where the token bucket and fair queueing of U3.6 play the same role between machines that weighted arbitration plays between cores. Emerging Trends in Network On Chips: three-dimensional stacking with through-silicon vias, chiplets joined over an interposer, and photonic and wireless links on chip. In the advanced architecture course's outline, this unit continues "the theory of on-chip networks" of U14.16.

### T0935

- **Topics:** Week 11: Low power design: dynamic power α C V² f and its terms (activity factor, switched capacitance, supply voltage, clock frequency), static (leakage) power, the end of Dennard scaling and dark silicon; clock gating and power gating; dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) and the energy per task, which scales with V², against race-to-idle when leakage is large; power and energy metrics (energy per instruction, energy-delay product); thermal limits. Week 12: Reliability and Hardware Security: transient (soft) faults from particle strikes and permanent faults from wear-out; failure rate, FIT (failures per 10⁹ device-hours) and MTTF; architectural vulnerability factor; error-detecting and error-correcting codes (parity, Hamming single-error correction, SECDED) for caches and memory; redundancy by triple modular redundancy and redundant multithreading. Hardware security from the defender's side: cache timing channels described as an information-flow model (a secret-dependent access changes which set the attacker's probe finds evicted), and defences by partitioning, randomised mapping and constant-time code; trusted execution environments as a hardware boundary. The outline's "aspects of low-power design, hardware security, and reliability" is the scope of this unit; attacks and their deeper defences belong to U5.20 and U6.9.

### T0936

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Hamming (1950); Hsiao (1970) on SECDED codes; Mukherjee et al. (2003) on the architectural vulnerability factor; Esmaeilzadeh et al. (2011) on dark silicon; Kocher et al. (2019) on Spectre; recalled, not checked]* links to U6.9 and U5.20, which own attacks and defences; leakage in the explorer is modelled as proportional to V, a stated simplification.

(7) Decision: the memo states the expected cost and benefit of the recommended policy with an interval, the assumptions that would reverse it, and the checks that guard against the usual failures (leakage, survivorship, multiple comparisons, class imbalance).
